docs.title: Introduction to Using GPUs on High Performance Clusters (HPC)
docs.text:
The goal of this workshop is to show you how to run your software on GPUs as efficiently as possible, on a high performance computing system like Mahuika.

What does efficiency mean in this context? It specifically means how we can keep the GPU running at its maximum for your computational job or simulation.

Concretely, an efficient GPU job is one where:

  • The GPU is busy for most of the time you hold it.
  • You asked for a card your work fits in, and not a larger one.
  • You asked for roughly the CPU cores and memory you actually use.

Why is this important? GPU time is in limited supply, due to its demand for research applications like AI and simulations. For this reason GPU time is expensive and precious, and minimising the amount of time you need a GPU to complete your computational job is very important.

Mahuika is also a shared resource. We all want to use the GPUs for our research. Having efficient jobs makes you a good user of the platform, and leaves time for other researchers to do their research as well.

docs.title: Who should be attending this workshop
docs.text:
You should be attending this workshop if you are using or are interested in using GPUs on Mahuika or another High Performance Computing (HPC) system.

Specifically, this workshop will cover what you should consider and what tests you should run in order to optimise the efficiency of your GPU jobs.

docs.title: Flow of this workshop
docs.text:
The workshop is in five stages.

Stage 1: Getting started with GPUs — what a GPU is good for, and a first job that provably uses one:

Chapter Overview 1. Introduction What a GPU is good at, and the ceiling on what it can do 2. Your first GPU job The lines that matter in a submit script, and a job to run 3. Is it really using the GPU? The checks that catch a job quietly running on the CPU

Stage 2: Asking for the right resources — the three decisions in your submit script:

Chapter Overview 4. Which GPU: precision The cards, and why double precision rules some of them out 5. Which GPU: will it fit? GPU memory, out-of-memory errors, and the smallest card that fits 6. How many CPUs do I need? Feeding the GPU, and where to start 7. How much CPU memory should I request? What a GPU job uses RAM for, and how to size it

Stage 3: Measuring your GPU jobs — finding out what your request actually did:

Chapter Overview 8. Measuring a GPU job A test submit script, seff, profile_plot and nvtop

Stage 4: Running interactive jobs — trying things on a GPU as you go:

Chapter Overview 9. Running interactive sessions with GPUs Holding a GPU with a job that waits, and debugging inside it

Stage 5: Putting it all together — turning the measurements into a request you keep:

Chapter Overview 10. Putting it all together The whole loop on one job: watch it, size the card, tune cores and memory Summary and checklist Everything, on one page, to take away

Beyond the basics — for after the workshop, when you set up your own work:

Page Overview B1: Getting your software running on a GPU Modules, Python environments, containers, and builds too old for the card B2: Where the time goes Measuring the CPU and GPU parts of a job, and reading data quickly B3: Long jobs Time limits, checkpoints, and why a job is pending B4: More than one GPU, and less than one When a second GPU helps, and what to do with small jobs

Reference: commands and the GPUs on this cluster.

Getting started

You should be comfortable in a Unix shell — cd, ls, editing a file — and have submitted a Slurm job before, or be willing to pick it up here. If you have not, the cluster's Submitting your first job tutorial is the place to start. No GPU experience is assumed.

Everything is done from a terminal on Mahuika, in OnDemand or over ssh. The exercise files live in ~/gpu-training. If you do not have them yet, copy them from the workshop's repository:

git clone https://github.com/nesi/reannz-intro-gpu-workshop.git
cp -r reannz-intro-gpu-workshop/examples ~/gpu-training
cd ~/gpu-training
ls

You can also read them on GitHub.

The exercises use PyTorch from the cluster's modules. The job scripts load it themselves. To run Python in a terminal of your own, load it there first:

module load PyTorch/2.13.0-foss-2026-Python-3.14.4-CUDA-13.2.1

Attribution Notice

  • Draws on the NeSI support documentation for Using GPUs and Hardware.
  • seff and svisit are documented as they behave in nesi/opt-nesi-bin.

docs.title: R1: Command reference
docs.text: Every command used in the workshop, with the flags that matter.

docs.title: sbatch
docs.text:
sbatch job.sl                    # submit
sbatch --parsable job.sl         # submit, print only the job ID
JOBID=$(sbatch --parsable job.sl)
sbatch --cpus-per-task 4 job.sl  # override a directive from the command line

Command-line options beat #SBATCH directives in the file.

docs.title: #SBATCH directives
docs.text: Directive Asks for --job-name NAME A name, so you can find it in squeue --account CODE The project to charge --time DD-HH:MM:SS Wall-clock limit. The job is killed at this point --cpus-per-task N CPU cores --mem 8GB System RAM (not VRAM) --mem-per-cpu 2GB RAM per core, instead of a total --gpus-per-node TYPE:N GPUs, by type --constraint a100_40gb Which A100: a100_40gb or a100_80gb --output FILE-%j.out Where output goes. %j is the job ID --qos debug High priority, strict limits, one job at a time (Debug QoS) --profile task Record resource use for profile_plot --acctg-freq 1 Take those records once a second --dependency=afterok:ID Start only once job ID has succeeded

docs.title: squeue
docs.text:
squeue --me                  # your jobs
squeue --me -t R             # just the running ones
squeue -j 12345              # one job
squeue --me -h               # no header (-h is NOT --help here)
squeue --me --start          # when pending jobs should start

ST column: PD pending, R running, CG completing. For a pending job, the last column gives the reason it is waiting — see B3: Long jobs.

docs.title: scancel
docs.text:
scancel 12345                # one job
scancel -u $USER             # all of yours

docs.title: scontrol
docs.text: scontrol show job 12345      # everything Slurm knows about a job

docs.title: nvidia-smi
docs.text:
nvidia-smi                                          # the table
nvidia-smi -L                                       # just list the devices
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv --loop=5

Useful --query-gpu fields: name, memory.total, memory.used, memory.free, utilization.gpu, utilization.memory, temperature.gpu, power.draw, compute_cap.

Warning

nvidia-smi is a snapshot. Use it to confirm a GPU is present, not to judge whether one is busy.

docs.title: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
docs.text:
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"
Value Means 0 One GPU 0,1 Two empty No GPU was requested unset Not inside a Slurm job

docs.title: Asking your software
docs.text:
# PyTorch: is a GPU usable right now?
python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"

# PyTorch: is this even a GPU-capable build?
python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda)"
#   2.13.0        13.2   -> a CUDA build
#   2.13.0+cpu    None   -> a CPU-only build; it will never use a GPU

# TensorFlow
python -c "import tensorflow as tf; print(tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU'))"

docs.title: svisit
docs.text:
svisit                       # your most recent running job
svisit 12345                 # a specific job
svisit 12345 nvtop           # run a command instead of a shell
svisit -t 12345              # show the srun command, do not run it

A wrapper around srun --pty --overlap --jobid=....

docs.title: nvtop
docs.text:
nvtop
Key Does q Quit F2 Setup F6 Sort the process list F9 Kill a process + / - Change the graph's time window

docs.title: A job that waits
docs.text:
sbatch hold-gpu.sl           # a job whose only command is: sleep infinity
svisit 12345                 # a terminal inside it, as often as you like
svisit 12345 nvtop           # or straight into a command
exit                         # leave the terminal - the job carries on
scancel 12345                # end the job, and give the GPU back

The GPU is held from the moment the job starts until scancel or the time limit, whether you are using it or not.

docs.title: srun --pty
docs.text:
srun --gpus-per-node l4:1 --cpus-per-task 2 --mem 4GB --time 00:15:00 --pty bash

Asks for the GPU and puts you inside the job in one step. It ends when you exit — or when your connection drops. Not available in the training environment.

docs.title: How to request each
docs.text:
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:1
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_40gb       # the 40 GB A100

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:1
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_80gb       # the 80 GB A100

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node h100:1

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node pro_6000:1

Without the constraint, an a100 request can land on either A100.

Ask for more than one only if your software says it can use more than one.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
Double precision first

The L4 and RTX PRO 6000 should be avoided for double-precision (fp64) work. At fp64 the L4 is about twenty times slower than an A100, and the RTX PRO 6000 about five times, and nothing warns you — the job simply takes days instead of hours.

If your software needs fp64, your choice is A100 or H100, whatever else is true.

Otherwise, by what you need:

Situation Card fp32 or fp16, fits in 24 GB L4 — shortest queue, plenty for most work fp64, up to 40 GB A100 40 GB fp64, up to 80 GB, or four GPUs that talk to each other A100 80 GB fp64, the largest models H100 NVL fp32/fp16 and very large, or wants the most raw fp32 RTX PRO 6000 Not sure yet L4 — measure with seff, move up if it does not fit

Take the smallest card your work fits in. Small cards are more plentiful and less contended, so your job starts sooner, and you leave the large ones for work that needs them.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
TFLOPS is trillions of floating-point operations per second. It is a theoretical peak that no real program reaches, so treat it as a way to compare cards rather than a prediction. The ratios between cards are meaningful; the absolute values are not.

fp64 : fp32 is the ratio of double- to single-precision throughput, and it is the most decision-relevant number on this page. A 1:2 card does double precision at half its single-precision rate, which is as good as it gets. A 1:64 card does it about sixty times slower — these are cards whose lineage is graphics and machine learning, where fp64 is almost never wanted.

Memory bandwidth is how fast the GPU can move data in and out of its own memory. Many real workloads are limited by this rather than by arithmetic, so a card with more bandwidth can outperform one with a better TFLOPS number.

Compute capability is NVIDIA's version number for the hardware's features. Some software requires a minimum; it rarely affects which card you should choose.

Why the RTX PRO 6000 is the interesting one

It has the highest fp32 figure in the fleet by a wide margin — six times an A100 — and one of the lowest fp64 figures.

For machine learning it is outstanding. For a quantum chemistry or CFD code it is one of the worst choices available. The same card, for the same money, depending entirely on what you run on it. That is the clearest illustration there is of why precision matters.

docs.title: 7. How much CPU memory should I request?
7. How much CPU memory should I request?
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Know what a GPU job actually uses CPU memory for
  • Work out how much your job needs
  • Recognise a job that was killed for going over what it asked for

Questions

  • How much memory should I ask for?
  • My job died without printing an error. What happened?

This chapter is about CPU memory, RAM, which you ask for with --mem. GPU memory comes with the card (Which GPU: will it fit?), and the two have nothing to do with each other.

docs.title: What a GPU job needs CPU memory for
docs.text:
It is easy to assume that once the work is on the GPU, the CPU side barely matters. It still needs room for:

  • Data read from disk, before it has been prepared.
  • Batches waiting to be handed over. Recall from How many CPUs that several cores prepare batches at once — every batch sitting ready is sitting in CPU memory.
  • The copy made during a transfer. Moving data to the GPU does not free the CPU memory it came from; for a moment it exists in both places.
  • Whatever your program keeps CPU-side — results being accumulated, logs, arrays you have not released.
  • Files in /tmp or $TMPDIR. On Mahuika a job's temporary directory sits in RAM, so anything written there counts against --mem (B2: Where the time goes).

docs.title: How much does my job need?
docs.text:
This is very dependent on your program, what you are wanting to do, etc. The best way is to measure the peak amount of memory you needed

  1. Start with a large amount of RAM. For example 64 GBs of RAM
  2. Run a short 15 minute job.
  3. Read the peak usage afterwards, with seff (Measuring a GPU job).
  4. Ask for 20–30% above that peak from then on.

The margin matters. Peak usage varies a little between runs — a slightly larger input file, a different batch arriving first — so sizing exactly to a single measured peak leaves you being killed occasionally, for no reason you can see.

Do not over-request

Asking for 256 GB when you need 4 makes your job much harder to schedule, so it waits longer, and holds memory nobody else can use while you have it.

Over-requesting is not caution — it is just slower.

docs.title: What happens when you run out
docs.text:
Going over the memory you asked for does not produce a normal error. Slurm kills the job, so your program never gets the chance to complain — which is why this one is confusing the first time you meet it.

slurmstepd: error: Detected 1 oom_kill event in StepId=1234567.batch.
Some of the step tasks have been OOM Killed.

Sometimes that is all you get. The signs to look for:

What you see What it means The job stops abruptly, part-way through Killed rather than crashed No error from your own program It was not given the chance to raise one oom_kill event in the output file Slurm is telling you directly Exit code 137 The job was killed (128 + signal 9) seff reports memory efficiency near or above 100% You used everything you asked for

Ask for more, then measure again and settle on a value with some headroom. If your request is already large, look instead for something you are holding on to CPU-side that you meant to release, or reduce your core count so that fewer batches are in flight at once.

Keypoints

  • A GPU job still needs real CPU memory: for data read from disk, for batches waiting to be handed over, and for the copy made during each transfer.
  • CPU memory and cores are linked. More cores means more batches in flight, which means more memory.
  • There is no formula — measure a short run, then add 20–30%.
  • Over-requesting delays your own job as well as everyone else's.
  • Running out gets your job killed, usually with no error from your program. Look for oom_kill or exit code 137.

docs.title: 2. Your first GPU job
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Know which #SBATCH lines a GPU job needs
  • Know which of them are real decisions, and where each is explained
  • Submit a GPU job, and read what it was given

Questions

  • What goes in a GPU submit script?
  • Which lines actually matter?

docs.title: A submit script for a GPU job
docs.text:
Consider that you have a program that you would like to run on one or several GPUs. A submit script like the one below will let you do that:

#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name      my-gpu-job
#SBATCH --account       nesi99991
#SBATCH --time          00:15:00
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1      (1)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 4         (2)
#SBATCH --mem           32GB      (3)
#SBATCH --output        my-job-%j.out

# Write the commands for running your GPU job in here
  1. The decision. Which GPU, and how many.
  2. A decision. CPU cores, which feed the GPU.
  3. A decision. System RAM — not GPU memory.

Three lines in this script are real decisions, and the next part of the workshop is about getting each of them right:

  • --gpus-per-node: which GPU should you choose?
  • --cpus-per-task: how many CPUs should you ask for?
  • --mem: how much memory should you ask for?

Briefly, here is what each one is for.

docs.title: --gpus-per-node — which GPU
docs.text:
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node <type>:<how many>

The type of GPU, and how many of them. Different cards differ by more than speed: they have different amounts of memory, and some are dramatically slower at double-precision arithmetic than others. Getting this wrong is the single most expensive mistake available, and it produces no error message.

Always name the type. Leaving it out gets you whatever happens to be free, which makes runs impossible to compare with one another. (The two A100s share a type, and need a --constraint as well.)

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1

Ask for one. Request more only if your software explicitly documents that it can use more than one — most cannot, and a second GPU it ignores sits idle for the whole job while somebody else waits for it.

→ Which GPU: precision and Which GPU: will it fit?

docs.title: --cpus-per-task — how many CPU cores
docs.text:
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 4

CPU cores for the job. A GPU job still needs them: the GPU cannot fetch its own work, so the CPU reads and prepares every batch before the GPU sees it. Too few cores and the GPU spends most of its time waiting.

→ How many CPUs do I need?

docs.title: --mem — how much system memory
docs.text:
#SBATCH --mem 8GB

Ordinary system RAM, attached to the CPU. This is not the memory on the GPU, which you cannot request at all — it comes with whichever card you chose. Confusing the two is the most common source of "I asked for more memory and it did not help".

→ How much CPU memory should I request?

docs.title: Run one
docs.text:
The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/first-job, and on GitHub.

Exercise: your first GPU job

cd ~/gpu-training/first-job
cat hello-gpu.sl
sbatch hello-gpu.sl
squeue --me

It takes a few seconds. Once squeue --me no longer lists it, read what it printed:

cat hello-gpu-<JobID>.out
What you should see 
Job 1234567 is running on g09
Slurm gave this job GPU number: '0'

followed by a table from nvidia-smi, with one card in it:

|   0  NVIDIA L4                      Off |   00000000:01:00.0 Off |                    0 |
| N/A   38C    P0             16W /   72W |       0MiB /  23034MiB |      0%      Default |

Two things to notice. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is 0: Slurm gave the job one GPU, and inside the job the GPUs it was given are numbered from 0. And nvidia-smi shows one card, the L4 the script asked for.

Neither of those proves that your program used it. That is the next chapter.

Keypoints

  • Three lines are the real decisions: --gpus-per-node, --cpus-per-task and --mem.
  • --gpus-per-node picks the card, and cards differ in memory and in double-precision speed, not just in speed.
  • A GPU job still needs CPU cores, because the CPU feeds the GPU.
  • --mem is system RAM. There is no flag for GPU memory — it comes with the card you pick.

docs.title: 5. Which GPU: will it fit?
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Work out whether your job will fit in a card's memory
  • Read an out-of-memory error, and know what to try first
  • Use the flow diagram to find the smallest card your work fits in

Questions

  • How much GPU memory does my job need?
  • My job ran out of GPU memory. Do I need a bigger card?

docs.title: GPU memory (VRAM)
docs.text:
GPU memory, also known as VRAM, is the memory on the GPU board itself, and it holds everything your program is working on there: a machine learning model's weights, the batch being processed, the results along the way. Each card has a different amount:

GPU Memory NVIDIA L4 24 GB NVIDIA A100 40 GB 40 GB NVIDIA A100 80 GB 80 GB NVIDIA H100 94 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB

Unlike CPU memory (RAM), which you ask for with --mem, you cannot ask for VRAM. You get all of it, on whichever card you chose. So it is important to choose the card that fits your work:

  • Avoid asking for a card with far more VRAM than you need.
  • If you only need 18 GB of VRAM, for example, an L4 is the right card. Asking for any other would be a poor use of resources.

Two GPUs is not more memory

Two 24 GB L4s are not a 48 GB card. Unless your software explicitly supports splitting a job across devices, the second GPU is a separate 24 GB your job cannot reach. Most software does not.

docs.title: How much does my job need?
docs.text:
It is often hard to work this out exactly, and the reliable answer comes from a short test run — Measuring a GPU job shows how to read it. But you can get close on paper, because every number your program holds on the GPU costs bytes:

Format Bytes per number fp64 8 fp32 4 bf16 / fp16 2

For training a neural network, a rough rule is four times the size of the model: the weights themselves, a gradient for each, and two optimiser states for each (Adam, the usual optimiser, keeps two). A model with a billion fp32 parameters is 4 GB of weights, so about 16 GB to train.

That is before the activations, the intermediate results of each batch, which grow with the batch size and can be larger than everything else put together. Treat four times the model as the floor, and measure.

docs.title: Running out of GPU memory
docs.text:
When a job asks for more than the card has, it stops with an error worth learning to read, because the useful part is not the part people look at:

torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 64.00 MiB. GPU 0
has a total capacity of 21.97 GiB of which 42.00 MiB is free. Including
non-PyTorch memory, this process has 21.93 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated
memory 21.62 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and 20.00 MiB is reserved by PyTorch
but unallocated. If reserved but unallocated memory is large try setting
PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True to avoid fragmentation.  See
documentation for Memory Management
(https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#optimizing-memory-usage-with-pytorch-cuda-alloc-conf)
Phrase Means Tried to allocate The allocation that failed — often small total capacity What the card has free What was left this process has What your process was holding, CUDA's own share included allocated by PyTorch How much of that is your program's data

The failed allocation is usually small

People see "Tried to allocate 64 MiB" and assume something strange has happened, because 64 MiB is nothing. The card was all but full; 64 MiB was the straw. The number that matters is what this process has.

docs.title: What to do when it does not fit
docs.text:
In this order:

  1. Check that it is not a leak. If GPU memory climbs a little with every step instead of staying level, the job is holding on to something it has finished with, and no card is big enough. Running interactive sessions has you watch both kinds of crash happen.
  2. Use a smaller batch, or a lower precision, if your software lets you choose and your work can tolerate it. Halving the batch roughly halves the activations, and bf16 halves everything stored in it (Which GPU: precision). Both change the work, so check your results still hold.
  3. Otherwise, move to the next card up. VRAM comes only with the card; there is no other way to ask for more.

Adding --mem will not help. That is CPU memory (How much CPU memory should I request?).

The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/gpu-memory, and on GitHub.

Exercise: fill a GPU until it refuses

cd ~/gpu-training/gpu-memory
sbatch vram.sl

It finishes in a few seconds. Read its output file, vram-<JobID>.out:

  1. In the first part, which counter moves when the script puts data in RAM, and which when it moves the data to the GPU?
  2. In the table, how much memory would a 1 billion parameter model need to train in fp32?
  3. At the end, find the out-of-memory error. How much did it try to allocate, and how much did the process already have?
What you should see
  1. Putting 32 MB in RAM moves only the RAM column. Moving it to the GPU moves only the VRAM column. Freeing the RAM copy changes nothing on the GPU. Two pools, not connected.
  2. About 15 GB: 3.7 GB of weights, times four.

  3. The card filled about 1.4 GB at a time, then:

    CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.41 GiB. GPU 0 has a total
capacity of 21.97 GiB of which 616.00 MiB is free. Including
non-PyTorch memory, this process has 21.37 GiB memory in use. Of
the allocated memory 21.08 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and 0 bytes
is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated. ...

    An allocation small next to what the card already held — the straw, not the load.

docs.title: Choosing your card
docs.text:
Memory and precision together decide the card. The figure below is the method:

  1. Determine which precision you need (Which GPU: precision). This decides which GPUs to try, and the order to try them in.

  2. Perform 15-minute test jobs on each GPU, in that order, until one is right:

    1. Did the job run out of GPU memory? Check that it is not a leak (above), then move to the next GPU up the ladder.
    2. Is the GPU sitting at 0% utilisation? Stop climbing — your program is not using the GPU at all, and a bigger one will not change that (Is it really using the GPU?).
    3. Record your GPU utilisation, GPU memory and step count. Do this before deciding anything, while the numbers are in front of you.
    4. Are you happy with how long the calculation took? If yes, this is your card — stop here. If not, move up one rung and run the 15 minutes again.

Why record the numbers before you decide

Step 4 is a judgement, and it is much easier to make with the previous rung's figures written down. "Is this fast enough?" is hard to answer in the abstract; "is this enough faster than the L4 to be worth the queue?" is not.

Measuring a GPU job covers reading those numbers off a finished job with seff, and the step count is what sets --time in Putting it all together.

If you would like a second opinion, pick_a_gpu.py in the same folder asks the same questions and prints a request: python3 pick_a_gpu.py.

Keypoints

  • There is no flag for GPU memory — you get all of whatever card you asked for, and two GPUs do not give you more.
  • Estimate on paper — about four times the model to train, plus the activations — then measure a short run.
  • The useful number in an out-of-memory error is what this process has, not what it tried to allocate.
  • When a job runs out: rule out a leak, then a smaller batch or lower precision, then the next card up. --mem never helps.
  • Take the smallest card that fits — shorter queue, fairer share, same result.

docs.title: 6. How many CPUs do I need?
6. How many CPUs do I need?
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Explain why a GPU job needs CPU cores at all
  • Pick a starting number, and know what measuring it will look like
  • Recognise that high CPU efficiency is not the goal
  • Tell CPU work that feeds the GPU from CPU work that only keeps the cores busy

Questions

  • I asked for a GPU. Why does the number of CPUs matter?
  • How do I pick a number?
  • My job does other CPU work in the background. Does that count?

docs.title: Why a GPU job needs CPUs
docs.text:
A GPU has to be given a batch of work by the CPU to perform. Every batch it processes has to be read from disk, decoded, filtered, reshaped and handed over, all on the CPU. So a GPU job is really two jobs taking turns:

This is one CPU core feeding one GPU. This is the worst arrangement available. Some points to take away from this arrangement:

  • The CPU never stops. It prepares batch 2 while the GPU is working on batch 1, then batch 3, and so on. Its track is solid the whole way across.
  • The GPU cannot start until a batch exists. The dotted arrows are the handovers. Batch 1 is not ready until the CPU has finished making it, which is why the GPU's first stretch is spent waiting rather than computing.
  • Computing is quicker than preparing here. So the GPU finishes each batch before the next one is ready, and has nothing to do in between. Those are the hatched gaps, and they are the whole problem.

There are two important points to take from this:

  • If preparing a batch takes longer than computing on it, the GPU spends more of the job waiting than working. Note that the GPU is the expensive half of the machine.
  • More cores let the preparation happen in parallel, which shortens each blue block and closes the gaps.

Conclusion: A GPU job with too few CPUs paid for a GPU and then starved it. It is probably the most common inefficiency in GPU work anywhere.

docs.title: What it looks like when the GPU is fed
docs.text:
Here is the same job again — same preparation cost, same computation cost — with four CPU cores instead of one:

Nothing about the GPU changed. What changed is that the four cores prepare four different batches at the same time, so batches now arrive faster than the GPU can get through them.

The GPU still waits for the very first batch — nothing can prevent that, since batch 1 does not exist until somebody makes it. But from that point on its track is solid, with no hatched gaps anywhere. Batches 2, 3 and 4 were finished by the other three cores long before the GPU needed them, and were sitting waiting.

This is what you are aiming for. Keep the GPU busy!

Both figures are a simplification

They show work flowing one way — the CPU prepares, the GPU computes — and stop there. Two things are deliberately left out.

Results coming back. Whatever the GPU produces has to return to the CPU at some point. In a training run that is almost nothing, because the model stays on the card and only a single number comes back each step. In a simulation it is periodic: forces, energies or a trajectory frame every so many steps.

Post-processing. Writing that frame out, checking convergence, updating a log — all of it runs on the CPU, and competes for the same cores as the preparation. A core busy writing the last result is not preparing the next piece of work.

This does not change the lesson: the CPU side has more to do than the pictures admit, so the cost of asking for too few cores is higher, not lower. But it does mean the blue blocks stand for everything the CPU does for the GPU, not only reading input.

docs.title: Work in the background
docs.text:
In the four-core picture, the cores do their work in the background: while the GPU computes one batch, they are already preparing the next ones. That is what keeps it fed, but only if your software prepares batches that way. In PyTorch, for example, it is the num_workers setting of a DataLoader, and the default, num_workers=0, prepares every batch in your main program, one at a time, however many cores you asked for.

Not everything running in the background feeds the GPU, though. The post-processing in the note above is one example; a job can be busy with plenty of CPU work that the GPU never waits for. Whether it matters to the GPU depends on what it is:

Running in the background Does the GPU need it? Preparing the next batches Yes. This is what feeds it Part of every step done on the CPU, such as some of the forces in a molecular dynamics code Yes. The GPU waits for it at the end of each step Writing results, checkpoints and logs No, though it takes cores from the work that does Another program started in the same job No, unless it makes something the GPU will use

Here is the four-core job again, with two of its cores taken by a CPU job running in the background:

All four cores are busy all of the time, so seff would report a CPU efficiency close to 100%. Yet the GPU is back to waiting, because only two of the four cores are making batches. Busy cores are not the same as a fed GPU.

Background work the GPU does not need still needs cores of its own:

  • If it has to happen in this job — writing the results, say — ask for its cores on top of the ones feeding the GPU.
  • If it does not — an analysis of earlier output, another program started alongside — run it as a separate CPU-only job. The cores on a GPU node are there to feed its GPUs.

docs.title: How many CPUs do I need for my job?
docs.text:
The number of CPU you need depends entirely on how much work your code does per batch before the GPU sees it, and that varies by orders of magnitude between applications. However, you can test how many CPUs you need by looking at the CPU and GPU efficiency as you change the number of CPU you use:

In this example, we hypothesis running the same job, but submitted with different numbers of cores:

Cores CPU efficiency GPU utilisation 1 100% 24% 2 81% 31% 4 64% 35% 8 38% 36% 16 20% 36%

Two things happen at once:

  • GPU utilisation climbs, then flattens. 24 → 31 → 35 → 36 → 36. The gain from 1 to 2 is large, 2 to 4 is smaller, and beyond 4 there is nothing left to gain. That flattening is the point you are looking for.
  • CPU efficiency falls the whole way. At one core the CPU is pinned at 100% trying to keep up. By four it is idle a third of the time, and by sixteen it is idle four-fifths of the time.

The last two rows are the important ones. Going from 4 cores to 16 is four times the CPU request for one percentage point of extra GPU use — cores that do nothing except make your job harder to schedule and eat into your fair share.

Ask for the smallest core count that gets GPU utilisation onto the flat part of the curve — here, 4.

Background work the GPU does not need shifts the whole curve to the right. If a background job took two cores, GPU utilisation would only stop climbing at about six, and CPU efficiency would look healthier in every row without the GPU being any busier. The GPU column is the one to trust.

Optional exercise: measure the curve yourself

Measure a small version of the table above: the same job at one, two and four cores. The scripts are also on GitHub.

cd ~/gpu-training/cpus
./scan-cpus.sh
squeue --me                # wait until all three have finished
./compare.sh

The three jobs take about a minute between them.

What you should see

Something like:

Cores CPU efficiency GPU utilisation 1 99% 25% 2 84% 39% 4 67% 48%

The same shape as the start of the table above: GPU utilisation climbs with every core added, while CPU efficiency falls. At four cores it is still climbing, if more slowly, so for this job you would keep going — 8, 16 — until it stops.

Keypoints

  • A GPU needs CPU cores to feed it. Too few, and it sits idle.
  • Start at --cpus-per-task 2, then measure.
  • Choose the smallest count where GPU utilisation stops climbing.
  • Falling CPU efficiency is the expected cost of a busier GPU, not a problem in itself.
  • Background CPU work only helps if the GPU needs it. Busy cores are not a fed GPU: give other work cores of its own, or a job of its own.
  • If more cores change nothing, the bottleneck is storage or the software — check that it prepares batches in the background.

docs.title: 9. Running interactive sessions with GPUs
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Know when an interactive session is the right tool, and when a batch job is
  • Hold a GPU with a job that waits, and work inside it with svisit
  • Use the session to debug a GPU job: check what you have, then watch it fail
  • Give the GPU back as soon as you are finished

Questions

  • How do I try things on a GPU without queueing a job for every attempt?
  • How do I get a terminal on a node with a GPU?
  • Why does it matter how long an interactive session lasts?

Everything so far has been batch jobs: write a script, submit it, wait, read what it did. That is the right way to run real work, and the only way to measure it. It is a slow way to find out why something does not work. Every attempt at a fix is another trip through the queue, and all that comes back is the last few lines of an output file.

An interactive session turns that round. You hold a GPU and work on it from a terminal: run something, watch what happens, change it and run it again, seconds apart rather than a queue apart.

docs.title: Batch or interactive?
docs.text:
Batch job Interactive session What you get back An output file, afterwards A terminal on the GPU's node, now Each attempt costs A trip through the queue Seconds The GPU is working While your program runs Only while you have something running Use it for Real work, and measuring it Checking, trying things, debugging

An interactive session is for finding out whether something works. A batch job is for running it, and for measuring how well it works — which is what the test job and the tools in Measuring a GPU job are for.

The GPU is yours for the whole session

From the moment the session starts until it ends, the GPU is held in your name: while your program runs, and just as much while you read its output, edit a file or go and make a coffee. Nobody else can use it, and every minute of it counts against your project.

That makes an interactive session the least efficient way there is to use a GPU. For debugging, which is short, that is a fair price. For anything else it is the opposite of what this workshop is for — so keep sessions short, and end them the moment you are done.

docs.title: A job that waits
docs.text:
The GPUs on Mahuika are on compute nodes, and the only way onto one is through a job. So an interactive session starts as an ordinary batch job — one whose only command is to wait:

#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name      hold-gpu
#SBATCH --account       nesi99991
#SBATCH --time          00:15:00    (1)
#SBATCH --qos           debug       (2)
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1        (3)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 2
#SBATCH --mem           4GB
#SBATCH --output        hold-gpu-%j.out

sleep infinity                      # (4)!
  1. How long you may hold the GPU. The session ends when this runs out, finished or not. Ask for long enough to try what you came to try, and no longer — you can always submit another.
  2. Start now. A session is only useful if you are there when it starts, and the debug QoS usually starts it within minutes. It allows one debug job at a time, and its rules say not to keep an interactive session open while you are not using it — especially one holding a GPU.
  3. The card to debug on. Ask for the same type your real job will use, so that what you find out applies to it.
  4. Wait. sleep does nothing and uses no CPU. It keeps the job, and its GPU, alive until you cancel it or the time limit ends it.

The job itself does no work. Everything happens in terminals you open inside it with svisit — the command you used in Measuring a GPU job to watch a running job with nvtop:

Step Command What it does 1 sbatch hold-gpu.sl Asks for the GPU 2 squeue --me Shows when it has started: ST is R 3 svisit <JobID> Opens a terminal inside the job, with its GPU 4 your commands Run, check and debug things on the GPU 5 exit Leaves that terminal. The job carries on 6 scancel <JobID> Ends the job, and gives the GPU back

svisit the same job as often as you like, from as many terminals as you like: run your program in one, and watch it with nvtop in another.

Why not srun --pty bash?

The cluster's documentation also describes a one-line interactive session:

srun --gpus-per-node l4:1 --cpus-per-task 2 --mem 4GB --time 00:15:00 --pty bash

That asks for the GPU and puts you inside the job in one step, and it works. The difference is what ties the job to you:

srun --pty bash A job that waits While it queues Your terminal waits with it Your terminal is free When you exit The job ends, and the GPU is freed You leave; the job carries on If your connection drops The job ends, with everything running in it Nothing happens. svisit back in

A laptop going to sleep, a dropped VPN or a closed browser tab is enough to end an srun session, unless you started it inside tmux. A job that waits does not notice. The price is that it does not notice you leaving either: exit is not scancel.

docs.title: Getting a session
docs.text:
The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/interactive, and on GitHub.

Exercise 1: hold a GPU and step inside it

Look first, from where you are now.

cd ~/gpu-training/interactive
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"

Ask for a GPU, and wait for the job to start.

cat hold-gpu.sl
sbatch hold-gpu.sl
squeue --me

Step inside, and look again — this time also asking the question that matters most, whether your software can see the card:

svisit <JobID>
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"
nvidia-smi -L
module load PyTorch/2.13.0-foss-2026-Python-3.14.4-CUDA-13.2.1
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"

Stay inside the job for the next exercise.

What you should see

Outside the job, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES prints nothing: you are not inside a job, so Slurm has given you no GPU.

Inside it, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0, nvidia-smi -L lists a single card, the L4 your job asked for, and PyTorch prints True. That is what being inside a job means: you see the GPU it was given, and nothing else.

If squeue shows the job as PD, it is still waiting for an L4. A small debug job usually starts within a few minutes.

docs.title: Debugging in the session
docs.text:
Two jobs died overnight, and both left the same error at the bottom of their output files:

torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory.

The same error is not always the same problem. The usual answer to running out of GPU memory is the next card up the ladder from Which GPU: will it fit?, but that only helps if the work is too big for the card. If the job is holding on to memory it has finished with — a leak — a bigger card just takes longer to fill.

An output file tells you where a job died. A session lets you watch it happen, as many times as you like, seconds apart.

Exercise 2: two crashes, watched live

Open a second terminal on Mahuika, beside the first so that you can see both. In it, visit the same job, straight into nvtop:

svisit <JobID> nvtop

nvtop shows your job's card, the L4.

In the first terminal, still inside the job, run the first crash and watch the GPU memory graph:

python3 crash_one.py

Then the second:

python3 crash_two.py

For each one, note how far it got before it died, and what GPU memory did on the way:

crash_one.py crash_two.py How far it got What GPU memory did Too big for the card, or a leak? What you should find crash_one.py crash_two.py How far it got 17 steps of work, then died on step 18 Died loading the model, at layer 9 of 10, before doing any work What GPU memory did Climbed with every step, until it hit the top Filled up while the model loaded Too big for the card, or a leak? A leak Too big

crash_two.py is too big for the card. Its model has ten layers and the card holds eight, so it was never going to fit, and the answer is the next card up the ladder.

crash_one.py is a leak. Every step does the same work, and should need no more memory than the one before. Instead it keeps every batch it has finished with, so memory climbs until there is none left. A bigger card would not save it — a leak fills any card in the end; a bigger one only takes longer. The fix is in the program, for whoever wrote it: you, or its developers.

Now compare the last line each one printed:

Tried to allocate This process had Free crash_one.py 1.1 GiB 21.9 GiB 100 MiB crash_two.py 2.7 GiB 21.9 GiB 89 MiB

Almost identical. Both died asking for a little more, on a card that was already full. The error tells you where a job died, not how it got there — watching it is what told the two apart.

A short test would have passed

Run the leak again, as a five-step test:

python3 crash_one.py --steps 5

It finishes without complaint, and GPU memory climbs the whole time. A leak passes a short test and kills the long run hours later. Memory that climbs while the work stays the same is the warning — in nvtop here, or in the GPU memory panel of profile_plot for a batch job (Measuring a GPU job).

docs.title: Giving the GPU back
docs.text:
When it works — or when you know why it does not — stop. Put what you learned into a batch script, like the test script from Measuring a GPU job, and end the session.

Exercise 3: give the GPU back

Press q in the second terminal to quit nvtop. In the first, leave the job, then end it:

exit
squeue --me
scancel <JobID>
squeue --me
seff <JobID>
What you should see

After exit, squeue --me still shows the job running: leaving it does not end it. Only scancel does, and the second squeue --me is empty.

seff reports the job as CANCELLED, with GPU lines something like these:

Peak GPU Utilisation:   0%
Peak GPU Memory Util:  95%  21.89 GB of 23 GB

The memory line is crash_two.py filling the card. The utilisation line is the whole session, and it is close to zero: for almost all the time you held the GPU, it did nothing — you were reading, typing and thinking. That is normal for debugging, and it is why a session should last minutes, not hours.

Had you forgotten to scancel, the job would have held an idle L4 until its fifteen minutes ran out, and ended as TIMEOUT.

Keypoints

  • An interactive session is for finding out whether something works. Running it, and measuring how well, is what batch jobs are for.
  • Hold a GPU with a job that waits — a normal #SBATCH header and sleep infinity — then svisit <JobID> for a terminal inside it.
  • svisit the job from as many terminals as you like: run your program in one, and watch it with nvtop in another.
  • The GPU is yours for the whole session, busy or not. Keep --time short, and use --qos debug so that it starts while you are there.
  • exit leaves the job; scancel ends it. Until you scancel, the card sits idle in your name.
  • The same out-of-memory error can be two problems. Too big for the card: the next card up. Memory climbing step after step: a leak, which no card will fix.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Describe, in one sentence, the kind of work a GPU is good at
  • Recognise the kinds of research work that do and do not benefit
  • Understand that "has GPU support" is a property of your software, not of your problem
  • Know that a GPU can only speed up the part of a job that runs on it

Questions

  • Why is a GPU faster than a CPU for some things and slower for others?
  • How do I find out whether my software can use one?
  • How much faster can a GPU make my job?

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A CPU has a small number of powerful cores that can each do something different. A GPU has thousands of weak cores that all have to do the same thing at the same time, to different data.

That is the whole trade-off. If your work is "apply this identical operation to ten million numbers", a GPU will do it in one pass while a CPU grinds through it. If your work is "do this, then decide what to do next based on the answer", the GPU's thousands of cores have nothing useful to do and you would have been better off on the CPU.

CPU GPU Cores tens thousands Each core fast, independent, good at branching slow, must march in step Good at decisions, sequences, one thing at a time the same arithmetic over huge arrays Bad at doing a million identical things at once anything that branches or waits

A useful mental image

A CPU is a handful of professors. A GPU is a stadium full of first-year students who all have to be given the same instruction at once.

If the job is "mark 50,000 identical multiple-choice papers", the stadium wins easily. If the job is "read this thesis and decide whether it passes", the stadium is useless no matter how many people are in it.

docs.title: What this means for research work
docs.text:
Work that usually benefits

  • Training and running neural networks
  • Molecular dynamics (GROMACS, AMBER, NAMD, LAMMPS)
  • Large dense linear algebra
  • Image and volume processing, where the same filter hits every pixel
  • Monte Carlo simulation with many independent samples
  • Genomics basecalling and alignment tools written for GPUs

Work that usually does not

  • Anything dominated by reading and writing files
  • Small problems. Moving data to the GPU costs time; if the calculation is short, you spend longer on the transfer than you save
  • Code with lots of branching and decisions, or where each step depends on the last
  • Software that has no GPU support — which is most software

The most important point on this page

A GPU does not speed up your work. GPU-aware software speeds up your work.

There is no setting that makes an ordinary program use a GPU. If your software was not written to use one, requesting a GPU does nothing at all except make your job wait longer in the queue and take a card away from someone who needed it.

Before requesting a GPU for the first time, find the page in your software's documentation that says it supports GPUs, and find out what you have to do to switch it on. It is usually a flag, a config setting, or a different executable name.

docs.title: How to find out about your own software
docs.text:
1. Search its documentation for "GPU" or "CUDA". Packages that support GPUs say so prominently, because it is a selling point.
  2. Check whether it needs to be switched on. Many packages have separate GPU and CPU builds, or need -gpu / --device cuda / use_gpu: true. Installing the GPU build is not the same as using it.
  3. Check the cluster's application pages. Widely used packages often have a support page with the exact settings — for example TensorFlow, AlphaFold, ABAQUS and ont-guppy-gpu.
  4. Ask the support desk. "Does X benefit from a GPU, and how do I turn it on?" is a question they answer often.

Getting a GPU build installed and working on the cluster is its own topic: B1: Getting your software running on a GPU.

docs.title: The ceiling
docs.text:
Even software that uses a GPU well only uses it for part of the job. Suppose 30% of your job's runtime is GPU work and 70% is reading files, preparing data and writing results. You swap the GPU for one twice as fast:

before:  [======== 70% CPU ========][=== 30% GPU ===]     100%
after:   [======== 70% CPU ========][ 15% ]                85%

You saved 15% of the runtime. Now swap it for one that is infinitely fast:

best:    [======== 70% CPU ========]                       70%

You saved 30%, and that is the most any GPU can ever do for this job.

The work that is not on the GPU sets a hard ceiling on what a better GPU can do for you. The pattern for what belongs on a GPU at all:

Belongs on the GPU Stays on the CPU The same arithmetic over large arrays Reading and writing files Matrix multiplication, convolution, FFT Decompressing, parsing, text handling Element-wise operations on big tensors Decisions and branching Many independent simulations at once Anything that must happen in order Neural network forward and backward passes Talking to a database or the network

Large, regular, identical, independent work belongs on the GPU. Everything else does not. B2: Where the time goes shows how to measure the split for your own job.

Exercise: before you go any further

Write down, for the software you actually use:

  1. Its name and version.
  2. Whether its documentation says it supports GPUs.
  3. What you have to change to switch that on.
  4. Which of its stages would run on the GPU, and roughly what share of the runtime they are.

If the answer to 2 is "no", the rest of this workshop is still worth knowing — you will need it the first time a package you use gains GPU support, and it will tell you how to check whether the claim is true.

docs.title: What the rest of this workshop does
docs.text:
Assuming your software does support GPUs, everything that follows is about getting a good one, confirming you got it, and finding out whether it helped.

Keypoints

  • A GPU does the same operation to very many pieces of data at once. That is the only thing it is better at.
  • Work that branches, waits on files, or is simply small will not go faster on a GPU — and may go slower.
  • Software has to be written to use a GPU. Requesting one does not make an ordinary program use it.
  • Check your software's documentation before you request a GPU, not after.
  • The work not on the GPU is a ceiling on what any GPU can do for your job.

docs.title: B3: Long Jobs and the Queue
B3: Long jobs: time limits, checkpoints and the queue
docs.text:
Beyond the basics

Not covered in the live workshop. Read it before you queue a GPU job that will run for more than a day.

Lesson Objectives

  • Choose a time limit from a measurement, not a guess
  • Know why a long GPU job should checkpoint, and what to save
  • Read why a job is pending, and know what makes one start sooner

Questions

  • How long should I ask for?
  • What happens when a job reaches its time limit?
  • My job has been pending for hours. Why?

docs.title: How long to ask for
docs.text:
Putting it all together set --time from the test job's step count: its rate, times the steps the real run needs, plus 20–30%. That margin matters, because of what happens at the limit:

  • Slurm stops the job when its time runs out, finished or not. seff reports it as TIMEOUT.
  • Everything since the job last saved its state is lost. For a three-day job that saves nothing until the end, that is three GPU-days.
  • No single job can run for longer than 21 days.

Asking for far too long is not free either. A longer job is harder for the scheduler to fit in, so it waits longer to start (more on that below).

docs.title: Checkpointing
docs.text:
A checkpoint is the job saving enough of its state to carry on from that point later. The cluster's advice is to checkpoint any job that runs longer than a day (Job checkpointing).

What to save is everything needed to carry on, and nothing else:

Kind of work What a checkpoint holds Training a model The model's weights, the optimiser's state, and the step count A simulation The program's own restart files. Most simulation codes write them, and can be told to start from one

How often is a trade: often enough that losing the time since the last one would not hurt, and rarely enough that writing it does not slow the job down. Every half hour to every few hours suits most jobs.

For PyTorch, the pattern is to save as you go, and to start from the last save if there is one:

import os
import torch

start = 0
if os.path.exists("checkpoint.pt"):
    saved = torch.load("checkpoint.pt")
    model.load_state_dict(saved["model"])
    optimiser.load_state_dict(saved["optimiser"])
    start = saved["step"] + 1

for step in range(start, total_steps):
    train_one_step(model, optimiser)
    if step % 1000 == 0:
        torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(),
                    "optimiser": optimiser.state_dict(),
                    "step": step}, "checkpoint.pt")

docs.title: Run it as a chain of shorter jobs
docs.text:
Once a job can pick up where it left off, it no longer has to be one long job. Split it into a chain, each link starting when the last one finishes:

sbatch train.sl                                 # Submitted batch job 1234567
sbatch --dependency=afterok:1234567 train.sl    # starts when that one succeeds

Shorter jobs start sooner, a failure costs you one link rather than the whole run, and a chain can run for longer than 21 days.

docs.title: Why is my job pending?
docs.text:
squeue --me gives the reason in its last column:

Reason Means What to do Priority Other jobs are ahead of yours Wait. A smaller, shorter request starts sooner Resources Your job is next, and is waiting for the cards, cores or memory it asked for to come free Wait, or ask for a card there are more of QOSMaxGRESPerUser You already hold as many GPUs as one person may at a time Wait for one of your own jobs to finish Dependency It is waiting for another job, as above Nothing; that is what you asked for

squeue --me --start shows when Slurm expects a pending job to start.

Each user may hold 6 GPUs at once, and 14 GPU-days' worth of running jobs — whichever comes first. The Job limits page has the full list.

docs.title: What makes a GPU job start sooner
docs.text:
• The smallest card that fits. There are more of them, and fewer people want them (Which GPU: will it fit?).
  • An honest --time. The scheduler fills gaps in the queue with jobs short enough to finish before the gap closes. A job that asks for a week cannot use a gap of a day.
  • Only what you use. Spare cores and memory make a job harder to place, for no benefit.

Keypoints

  • Set --time from the test job's step count, plus 20–30%. At the limit the job is stopped, finished or not.
  • Checkpoint any job longer than a day: save the state, and start from the last save if there is one.
  • A checkpointed job can run as a chain of shorter jobs, with --dependency=afterok.
  • squeue --me gives the reason a job is waiting. Smaller, shorter, honest requests start sooner.

docs.title: 8. Measuring a GPU job
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Set up a short test job that starts straight away
  • Turn on Slurm's profiling, so there is something to look at afterwards
  • Read a finished job with seff, and its shape over time with profile_plot
  • Watch a running job's GPU with nvtop

Questions

  • How do I run a test job without waiting all day for it?
  • Which command tells me what the GPU actually did?

The last four chapters were about what to ask for. Each one ended the same way — the only reliable answer comes from measuring:

Decision How you settle it Where Which GPU Climb the ladder until the job fits and runs fast enough Which GPU: will it fit? How many CPUs Add cores until GPU utilisation stops climbing How many CPUs How much RAM Measure the peak, then add 20–30% How much CPU memory

All three come down to one method: run something short, then look at what it did. This chapter is the tools that make that possible.

docs.title: A submit script for testing
docs.text:
A test job is not a normal job. You want it to start now, run briefly, and record everything — none of which you want for production work.

#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name      gpu-test
#SBATCH --account       nesi99991
#SBATCH --time          00:15:00    (1)
#SBATCH --qos           debug       (2)
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 4
#SBATCH --mem           32GB
#SBATCH --profile       task        (3)
#SBATCH --acctg-freq    1           (4)
#SBATCH --output        gpu-test-%j.out

# your program here
  1. Fifteen minutes. Long enough for the job to settle into its normal rhythm, short enough that a bad guess costs you very little.
  2. Debug priority, so the test starts within minutes.
  3. Profile this job, so Slurm records what it did over time.
  4. Sample once a second, rather than the much coarser default.

The last three lines exist only for testing. Take them out of your production scripts.

docs.title: --qos debug — jumping the queue
docs.text:
The debug QoS raises your job's priority so that it starts quickly, in return for strict limits on its size and length. It is meant for exactly this kind of one-off test:

#SBATCH --qos debug
#SBATCH --time 00:15:00

You can only have one debug job at a time. The Debug QoS page has the limits, and what it must not be used for.

docs.title: --profile task and --acctg-freq 1 — recording what happened
docs.text:
--profile task tells Slurm to measure the CPU, GPU and memory your job uses over time, rather than only summing it up at the end. --acctg-freq 1 tells Slurm to take those measurements every second.

#SBATCH --profile task
#SBATCH --acctg-freq 1

docs.title: Watching a running job
docs.text:
Once your test job is running, you can watch its GPU live:

  1. Find its job ID with squeue --me.

    user.name@login03:$ squeue --me
JOBID         USER     ACCOUNT   NAME        CPUS MIN_MEM PARTITI START_TIME     TIME_LEFT STATE    NODELIST(REASON)
1234567       user.nam nesi99999 Example_GPU_   8     24G genoa   Apr 30 17:36    23:58:08 RUNNING  g09

  2. Step onto the node the job is running on with svisit <JobID>.

    user.name@login03:$ svisit 1234567
user.name@g09:$

  3. Run nvtop, which shows the job's GPU utilisation and memory as they happen.

Press q to quit nvtop, and exit to come back to the login node.

docs.title: seff: one number per resource
docs.text:
Once the job has finished, seff summarises what it used:

seff <JobID>

For a fifteen-minute test on an L4, it looks like this:

Job ID: 1234567
State: TIMEOUT
Tasks: 1
Cores: 4
Job Wall-time:        100%  00:15:04 of 00:15:00 time limit
Avg CPU Utilisation:   98%  00:59:20 of 01:00:16 core-walltime
Peak Mem Utilisation:   1%  284.46 MB of 32.00 GB
Peak GPU Utilisation:  43%
Peak GPU Memory Util:   2%  510.00 MB of 23 GB

Read it against the decisions you made:

Line What it is telling you Which request it judges Job Wall-time How much of your time limit you used --time Avg CPU Utilisation How busy the cores you asked for were --cpus-per-task Peak Mem Utilisation Peak CPU memory against what you asked for --mem Peak GPU Utilisation How much of the job the GPU was working --cpus-per-task, and your code Peak GPU Memory Util Peak GPU memory against what the card has --gpus-per-node

No GPU lines at all means the job had no GPU.

docs.title: profile_plot: the same job, over time
docs.text:
seff gives one number per resource, and for utilisation that number is an average over the whole job, whatever the "Peak" in its name suggests. A job holding a steady 40% and a job swinging between 100% and 0% both average 40%, and they have completely different causes. To tell them apart, plot the job over time. Because the test script used --profile task:

profile_plot <JobID>

This writes a file called <JobID>_profile.png, which looks something like this:

Panel What it shows CPUs How many cores were actually in use Memory (MB) RSS — real memory held — and VMSize, the address space reserved Cumulative I/O (MB) Bytes read (solid) and written (dashed), adding up over the run GPUs GPU utilisation, as a fraction of one card GPU Mem (MB) How much GPU memory the job was holding

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/measuring, and on GitHub.

Exercise: a test job, measured

Submit it. It runs for three minutes.

cd ~/gpu-training/measuring
cat test-job.sl
sbatch test-job.sl

Watch it while it runs.

squeue --me
svisit <JobID>
nvtop

Press q, then exit, once you have seen the shape.

Read it once it has finished.

seff <JobID>
profile_plot <JobID>

Then open the <JobID>_profile.png it writes.

What you should see

In nvtop, GPU utilisation rises and falls on a regular beat: twenty seconds of work, ten seconds of waiting. Then seff:

Job ID: 1234567
State: COMPLETED
Tasks: 1
Cores: 2
Job Wall-time:         20%  00:03:03 of 00:15:00 time limit
Avg CPU Utilisation:   67%  00:04:05 of 00:06:07 core-walltime
Peak Mem Utilisation:  13%  522.78 MB of 4.00 GB
Peak GPU Utilisation:  65%
Peak GPU Memory Util:   3%  648.00 MB of 23 GB

The job used three of its fifteen minutes, and about two thirds of the GPU — which seff reports as a single 65%. The plot shows where that number comes from: the GPU panel is a sawtooth, high for twenty seconds and idle for ten. That shape is what an average hides.

The GPU memory is more than the 64 MB the script holds: PyTorch keeps memory it has finished with for reuse, and CUDA itself takes a few hundred MB in any job that uses the GPU.

Keypoints

  • A test job wants --time 00:15:00 and --qos debug so it starts straight away. Take the debug QoS out again afterwards.
  • --profile task with --acctg-freq 1 records what the job did second by second. Testing only — never in a production script.
  • seff <JobID> after the job gives one number per resource, and each one judges a request you made.
  • profile_plot <JobID> turns that into a graph over time. The average and the shape are different information.
  • squeue --me → svisit <JobID> → nvtop to watch a job live.

docs.title: B4: More Than One GPU, and Less Than One
B4: More than one GPU, and less than one
docs.text:
Beyond the basics

Not covered in the live workshop.

Lesson Objectives

  • Know when a second GPU can help, and how to find out whether it does
  • Know which nodes suit work that passes data between GPUs
  • Know what to do with work too small for a whole GPU

Questions

  • Will two GPUs make my job twice as fast?
  • My job uses only a fraction of the card. What should I do?

docs.title: More than one GPU
docs.text:
A second GPU helps only if your software splits the work between them. The common ways it does:

  • Data parallel training. Each GPU holds a copy of the model and trains on different batches, and the GPUs combine what they learned after every step. In PyTorch this is DistributedDataParallel, started with torchrun.
  • Simulation codes that divide the system, as several molecular dynamics codes can.
  • Splitting a model too big for one card across several. Only software written to do this can.

If your software does none of these, the second GPU sits idle for the whole job — and two cards are still not one bigger card (Which GPU: will it fit?).

docs.title: Find out whether it helps
docs.text:
Measure, as with everything else: run the same test job on one GPU and on two, and compare the throughput — steps per second, or whatever your program counts. For example:

GPUs Steps per second Speed-up Efficiency 1 100 1.0× 100% 2 185 1.85× 93% 4 300 3.0× 75%

Efficiency is the speed-up divided by the number of GPUs. Here two GPUs are well worth it; four are already wasting a quarter of what they hold. A useful rule: each GPU you add should earn its place, and once efficiency falls much below 75%, the extra GPUs are mostly waiting while somebody else waits for them.

docs.title: How to ask, and where
docs.text:
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:2
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_80gb
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 8              # cores for each GPU, times two

Two things decide where multi-GPU work should run:

  • How many GPUs a node has. All the GPUs of one job are on one node unless you go further than this page does: up to four L4s or 80 GB A100s, three 40 GB A100s, or two H100s or RTX PRO 6000s.
  • How the GPUs talk to each other. The four GPUs on each 80 GB A100 node are linked by NVLink. Every other card, the H100s included, talks over PCIe, which is much slower for GPU-to-GPU traffic. Work that exchanges data between GPUs every step belongs on the 80 GB A100s (Hardware).

The per-user limit applies to the total: six GPUs at once (B3).

docs.title: Less than one GPU
docs.text:
The opposite problem is more common. If seff shows a job using a small fraction of its card — GPU memory well under 25%, and utilisation low — the card is too big for it. In order of what to try:

  1. The smallest card. An L4 is often enough (Which GPU: will it fit?).

  2. More work in each job. If several independent pieces of work fit in the GPU's memory together, run them on the same GPU at the same time, in the background of one job:

    python3 run.py --input part-1 &
python3 run.py --input part-2 &
python3 run.py --input part-3 &
wait

    Each one is background work the GPU needs, so each needs cores of its own (How many CPUs).

  3. Many separate jobs, if the pieces really are independent: a job array (#SBATCH --array=1-100) runs one job per piece. Each still holds a whole GPU, so make each piece worth one — or combine this with 2.

Keypoints

  • A second GPU helps only if your software splits the work. Most does not.
  • Measure throughput on one GPU and on two. Each GPU you add should earn its place.
  • Work that passes data between GPUs every step belongs on the 80 GB A100s, the only GPUs on the cluster linked by NVLink.
  • A job using a fraction of a card should use a smaller card, or do more on the one it has.

docs.title: 4. Which GPU: precision
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Know which GPUs Mahuika has, and how to ask for each one
  • Decide whether your work needs double precision, and what that rules out
  • Know when lower precision is worth using for machine learning

Questions

  • What GPUs can I ask for?
  • My job runs on all of them. Does it matter which one I choose?

docs.title: The GPUs available on Mahuika
docs.text:
We have a number of GPUs available on Mahuika for scientific research. These GPUs, and how you ask for each of them, are below:

GPU Per node Total on Mahuika Request NVIDIA L4 4 16 l4:1 NVIDIA A100 40 GB 3 6 a100:1 + --constraint=a100_40gb NVIDIA A100 80 GB 4 16 a100:1 + --constraint=a100_80gb NVIDIA H100 2 8 h100:1 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 2 8 pro_6000:1

Asking for a particular A100

Both A100s have the same Slurm name, a100, so --gpus-per-node a100:1 on its own can land on either of them. Choose which with --constraint (Using GPUs):

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:1
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_40gb     # the 40 GB A100

#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:1
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_80gb     # the 80 GB A100

Leaving the constraint out is the same mistake as leaving out the type in your first GPU job: you get whichever is free, and runs you cannot compare — or 40 GB of memory when your job needed 80.

Optional exercise: ask for each A100

Ask for each A100 in turn, and watch the constraint choose between them. --wrap runs a single command as a job, with no script:

cd ~/gpu-training/precision
query="nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader"
sbatch --gpus-per-node a100:1 --constraint a100_40gb --wrap "$query"
sbatch --gpus-per-node a100:1 --constraint a100_80gb --wrap "$query"

Each job writes one line to its slurm-<JobID>.out.

What you should see 
NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB, 40960 MiB
NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB, 81920 MiB

Both jobs asked for a100:1. The constraint is what decided that one got the 40 GB card and the other the 80 GB.

docs.title: Two questions decide the card
docs.text:
1. Does your software use single or double precision? Get this wrong and the job runs perfectly correctly, just many times slower than it should. That is this chapter.
  2. Will your job fit in the card's memory? If it does not, the job cannot run there at all. That is the next chapter.

Precision comes first, because it rules cards in or out. Memory then picks between what is left.

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
What is precision?

Precision is how many significant figures a number is stored with.

Why is precision important?

  1. For some calculations, having too few significant figures introduces errors that build up over many iterations. It only affects some kinds of calculation.
  2. Different GPUs run different precisions at very different speeds.

There are two precision types to focus on:

Format Also called Significant digits Bytes float32 single precision, fp32 ~7 4 float64 double precision, fp64 ~16 8

Which precision type does my software use?

It depends on what your software was written for.

  • fp32 is generally used for machine learning and AI, as well as for molecular dynamics.
  • fp64 is generally used where a high level of precision is needed, such as many chemistry and engineering codes where small errors can build up.
  • Always check your software's documentation to find out which it uses.

As a rough guide:

Usually needs fp64 Usually fine in fp32 Quantum chemistry (VASP, Gaussian, CP2K) Machine learning, training and inference Computational fluid dynamics Molecular dynamics (LAMMPS, GROMACS) Climate and ocean models Image and signal processing Iterative solvers, eigenvalue problems Most Monte Carlo work

Why does it matter which card?

Every GPU can do both kinds of calculation. What differs enormously is how fast. These are the calculation speeds (TFLOPS) of each card at REANNZ:

GPU fp32 fp64 NVIDIA L4 30.3 TFLOPS 0.5 TFLOPS NVIDIA A100 (40 GB and 80 GB) 19.5 TFLOPS 9.7 TFLOPS NVIDIA H100 60 TFLOPS 30 TFLOPS NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 120 TFLOPS 1.9 TFLOPS

A TFLOPS figure means little on its own, but the comparisons between cards and between precisions do:

  1. For fp32 work, the order is RTX PRO 6000 > H100 > L4 > A100.

    If you run machine learning or other fp32 work, this is the order of cards to consider for speed. The L4 beats the A100 here, though its 24 GB of memory may be too small for your job — that is the next chapter.

  2. At fp64, the L4 and RTX PRO 6000 fall far behind.

    Each does fp64 at about a sixtieth of its own fp32 speed. Against an A100, the L4 is about twenty times slower at fp64 and the RTX PRO 6000 about five times, and the H100 is three times faster again. If your work needs double precision, your choice is the A100 or the H100, whatever else is true.

Do not run double-precision jobs on the L4 or RTX PRO 6000

An eight-hour double-precision job on an A100 would take about a week on an L4. You will not see an error message for this, so watch out.

Some final pointers

  • If your software can use fp32, use it over fp64. fp32 calculations are generally much faster than fp64.
  • If your software performs calculations where small errors compound over millions of steps, you will need fp64.

Lower precision for machine learning

fp32 and fp64 are not the only choices. Machine learning frameworks can also compute in bf16 or fp16, two bytes per number, and all four of Mahuika's GPU models have tensor cores that run these many times faster than ordinary fp32 arithmetic. They also support TF32, which runs fp32 matrix maths on the tensor cores.

In PyTorch, mixed precision is a block around your forward pass, and TF32 is one line:

torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")     # TF32 for fp32 matrix maths

with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    loss = model(batch)

Two bytes per number also means half the GPU memory, which can be the difference between fitting a card and not. Most training is fine in bf16, but check that your results are — and none of this is any use to software that needs fp64.

Optional exercise: watch fp32 go wrong

If you have time:

cd ~/gpu-training/precision
module load PyTorch/2.13.0-foss-2026-Python-3.14.4-CUDA-13.2.1
python3 accuracy.py
python3 show_fleet.py

accuracy.py shows fp32 losing accuracy in three ways you can check by hand, and show_fleet.py prints the published speeds of every card side by side.

Keypoints

  • Five things to ask for, differing in memory and in double-precision speed, not simply in how fast they are.
  • The A100 comes in 40 GB and 80 GB. They are the same chip at the same speed, and share the Slurm name a100 — choose with --constraint=a100_40gb or --constraint=a100_80gb.
  • Name the type, and ask for one unless your software can use more.
  • fp64 work belongs on an A100 or H100. At fp64 the L4 is about twenty times slower than an A100, and the RTX PRO 6000 about five, with no warning.
  • For machine learning, bf16 and TF32 run on the tensor cores, faster than fp32 and in half the memory.

docs.title: 10. Putting it all together
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Watch a running job and judge from the live display whether the GPU is busy
  • Use seff across a set of finished jobs to find the smallest card your work fits in
  • Use seff and profile_plot to settle the core count and the memory request
  • Write the answers back into a production submit script

Questions

  • I have the tools. How do I actually use them on a real job?
  • How do I know when I am finished tuning?

Everything so far has been one piece at a time. This chapter runs the whole loop, on one job, from first guess to a script you would keep.

This is the diagram from Which GPU: will it fit? again — it is the plan for this entire chapter:

We will work through it in three passes:

Pass Question Tool 1 Is the job using the GPU at all, and what does it look like? nvtop, live 2 Which card does it fit in? seff, across several finished jobs 3 How many cores and how much memory does it need? seff and profile_plot

docs.title: Pass 1: watch a job while it runs
docs.text:
Before measuring anything carefully, look at the job with your own eyes. It takes two minutes and it catches the failures that would make every later measurement meaningless.

The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/putting-it-together, and on GitHub.

Exercise 1: watch a job live

Submit the job.

cd ~/gpu-training/putting-it-together
cat watch-me.sl
sbatch watch-me.sl

Find it, and jump onto its node.

squeue --me
svisit <JobID>

Watch it.

nvtop

Leave it running for a minute and watch the two graphs. Then press q to quit, and exit to come back to the login node.

What you should see

A sawtooth. GPU utilisation climbs, drops back, climbs again — over and over, never settling high.

That shape is the starved GPU from How many CPUs, seen live. Each rise is the GPU working on a batch; each fall is the GPU waiting while the CPU prepares the next one.

GPU memory, meanwhile, will be flat. It was allocated at start-up and does not change.

What you are checking for at this stage is not a number, it is a category:

What the display shows What it means What to do Flat at zero, your process absent The job is not using the GPU Stop. Nothing below will help until that is fixed Sawtooth Starved between batches Continue, and fix it in pass 3 High and flat Already well fed Continue to pass 2 Memory climbing without limit A leak Fix the code before tuning anything

Only once the GPU is genuinely being used is there any point measuring how well it is being used.

75% is the right kind of full

A job filling 75% of its card has headroom for a slightly larger input without falling over, and is not wasting most of a scarce resource.

Below about 25%, look at the card underneath. Above about 90%, look at the card above — you are one bigger input away from the L4's fate.
