docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Exercise 3b: settle the memory request

Take the four-core job's report from exercise 3a, and look at the Peak Mem Utilisation line rather than the GPU ones:

Peak Mem Utilisation:  19%  6.20 GB of 32.00 GB
  1. What was the peak CPU memory this job actually used?
  2. What was requested?
  3. What should the request be, allowing 20–30% headroom?
Answer

The job peaked at 6.2 GB and asked for 32 GB — so 26 GB sat reserved and untouched for the whole run, making the job harder to schedule for no benefit.

6.2 GB plus 30% is about 8 GB. Ask for --mem 8GB.

Be careful not to size this from the one-core run. Memory scales with the core count (How much CPU memory) — measure it at the core count you have actually chosen.

docs.title: Writing the answers back
docs.text: Three passes, three answers, and one more to work out: how long to ask for.

docs.title: How long to ask for
docs.text:
The flow diagram had you record a step count in the 15-minute test, and this is what it is for. If the test got through 1,250 steps in 15 minutes and the real run needs 30,000, the run will take about 24 times as long: six hours. Add 20–30% for the variation a single test will not show you, and ask for eight.

Put it all in a script you would keep:

#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name      my-real-job
#SBATCH --account       nesi99991
#SBATCH --time          08:00:00      # (1)
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node a100:1        # (2)
#SBATCH --constraint    a100_40gb
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 4             # (3)
#SBATCH --mem           8GB           # (4)
#SBATCH --output        my-job-%j.out

# your program here
  1. The step count. The test's rate, times the steps you need, plus a margin. Past a day, read B3: Long jobs and checkpoint.
  2. Pass 2. The smallest card the job fits in: the 40 GB A100, which takes a constraint (Which GPU: precision).
  3. Pass 3a. Where GPU utilisation stopped climbing.
  4. Pass 3b. Measured peak, plus headroom.

Take the testing lines out

--qos debug, --profile task and --acctg-freq=1 all belong to the 15-minute test job and none of them belong here.

Leaving --qos debug in a production script will get the job killed at the debug walltime limit. Leaving the profiling on writes a sample every second for the entire run.

And --time comes from the step count, not from the 15 minutes the test needed.

Keypoints

  • Look before you measure. A minute with nvtop tells you whether the job is worth measuring at all.
  • Card first, then cores, then memory. The card decides what is possible; the other two decide how well it goes.
  • The smallest card that fits is the right card. 75% full is healthy; under 25% means try the card below.
  • Choose the core count where GPU utilisation stops climbing, not where CPU efficiency looks best.
  • Size memory from a run at the core count you have actually settled on.
  • Set --time from the test's step count, plus 20–30%.
  • Strip the testing flags before the script becomes a real job.

docs.title: B1: Getting your software running on a GPU
docs.text:
Beyond the basics

Not covered in the live workshop. Read it before you set up your own GPU software on the cluster — it is where most first GPU jobs go wrong, long before the choice of card matters.

Lesson Objectives

  • Know the three ways GPU software arrives on the cluster, and what each needs from you
  • Check that a build can use a GPU at all, and the GPU you asked for
  • Test new software in an interactive session rather than a queued job

Questions

  • Do I need to load a CUDA module?
  • My software works on one card and not on another. Why?

docs.title: Three ways to get GPU software
docs.text:
How you get it What you need to do about CUDA A module module spider and module load Nothing. The module loads the CUDA it was built with A Python environment pip install or conda Usually nothing. PyTorch and TensorFlow bring their own CUDA, so what you need is a GPU build, not a CUDA module A container apptainer pull, for example from NVIDIA's NGC registry Run it with --nv, or the container cannot see the GPU

Start with a module if there is one, and check the cluster's application pages first: widely used GPU packages often have a page with the exact settings.

You only need to load a CUDA module yourself when you are compiling GPU code, or when your software's instructions tell you to.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
module spider <name>                # which versions exist
module load <name>/<version>        # loads its CUDA along with it

docs.title: Python environments
docs.text:
Install a GPU build, not the default one. For PyTorch, the install command on pytorch.org names the CUDA version in its index URL, for example:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

Then check what you got, as in Is it really using the GPU?:

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda)"
#   2.14.0+cu128  12.8   -> a CUDA build
#   2.14.0+cpu    None   -> a CPU-only build; it will never use a GPU

Environments are large. Your home directory holds 20 GB, so put big environments in your project directory instead (Filesystems and quotas).

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
module load Apptainer
apptainer pull pytorch.sif docker://nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:<tag>
apptainer exec --nv pytorch.sif python my_script.py

Without --nv the container cannot see the GPU, and most software inside it quietly runs on the CPU — the same failure as forgetting --gpus-per-node. The cluster's NVIDIA GPU containers page has a worked example.

docs.title: Is the build new enough for the card?
docs.text:
Each generation of GPU has a compute capability, and a build only runs on the generations it was compiled for:

GPU Compute capability A100 8.0 L4 8.9 H100 9.0 RTX PRO 6000 12.0

The RTX PRO 6000 is the newest card, so it is the one older builds fail on. The error looks like one of these:

CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device
NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 ... with CUDA capability sm_120 is not compatible with the current PyTorch installation.

The fix is a newer build — for PyTorch, one built for CUDA 12.8 or later. The same software working on an A100 and failing on the RTX PRO 6000 is almost always this.

The node matters too. nvidia-smi shows, top right, the newest CUDA version its driver supports. A build made for a newer major version of CUDA than that fails with CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version. Within one major version a newer build still runs: the cluster's PyTorch module, built for CUDA 13.2, runs on a driver that shows 13.0.

docs.title: Test it in an interactive session
docs.text:
You can install software on the login node, but you cannot test it there: the GPUs are on the compute nodes. Test it in an interactive session on the card you intend to use:

  1. Hold a GPU with a job that waits, and svisit it.
  2. Load your module, activate your environment, or point at your container.
  3. Make the checks from Is it really using the GPU?.
  4. Run your program on the smallest input that does something real.
  5. exit, and scancel the job.

Ten minutes there saves a day of queueing jobs that fail at the first line.

If you write your own GPU code

Writing GPU code is beyond this workshop. If you want to see what it looks like, cuda_kernel.py has two small CUDA kernels written in Python with Numba. To compile CUDA code of your own with nvcc, load a CUDA module first.

Keypoints

  • Modules load their own CUDA. So do PyTorch and TensorFlow from pip or conda. Load a CUDA module yourself only to compile code.
  • Check you have a GPU build: +cu128, not +cpu.
  • A build must be new enough for the card. Failing on the RTX PRO 6000 and working on an A100 means the build is too old.
  • Containers need --nv to see the GPU.
  • Test in an interactive session, not in a queued job, and not on the login node.

docs.title: Summary and checklist
docs.text: Everything from the workshop, on one page.

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
Everything else exists to answer these.

# Question Measure it with Where 1 Is my job using the GPU at all? CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, your software's own check, seff's GPU lines Is it really using the GPU? 2 Does my software need double precision (fp64)? Its documentation Which GPU: precision 3 How much VRAM does my work need? Arithmetic, then seff Which GPU: will it fit? 4 How many CPU cores keep the GPU fed? Submit at several core counts and compare How many CPUs 5 What fraction of my runtime is on the GPU? seff, or timers around your stages Measuring a GPU job, B2

docs.title: A GPU job script, annotated
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash -e
#SBATCH --job-name      my-job
#SBATCH --account       nesi99991
#SBATCH --time          01:00:00     # the test job's step count, plus 20-30%
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task 4            # measured: the point GPU util stopped rising
#SBATCH --mem           8GB          # RAM. From seff's Peak Mem Utilisation
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1         # smallest card your work fits in
#SBATCH --output        my-job-%j.out

# Stop at once if there is no GPU, rather than running on the CPU for days.
[ -n "${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}" ] \
    || { echo "ERROR: no GPU allocated" >&2; exit 1; }

# Record what this job could see. Costs nothing, settles arguments later.
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader

module load <your software>          # it loads the CUDA it was built with
srun my_program --use-gpu

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
1. Check your software supports GPUs. Most does not. Requesting a GPU does not make a program use one.
  2. Request one, naming the type: --gpus-per-node l4:1. The two A100s also need --constraint=a100_40gb or --constraint=a100_80gb.
  3. Confirm you got it — CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is not empty, and your software reports a device, not just nvidia-smi. Better still, make the job fail when it has none.
  4. Test it short: fifteen minutes with --qos debug and --profile task.
  5. Watch it live the first time: squeue --me → svisit <jobid> → nvtop.
  6. Read seff afterwards. Every time.
  7. Adjust and repeat, then take the testing lines out and set --time from the step count.

docs.title: Which tool, when
docs.text: Question Tool Not Is there a GPU I can use? nvidia-smi Did my software find it? Ask the software nvidia-smi Is my software even GPU-capable? torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda Is it busy right now? nvtop, via svisit nvidia-smi — one sample proves nothing Was it busy overall? seff nvidia-smi Was it busy all the time, or in bursts? profile_plot seff — an average hides the shape Did this job have a GPU at all? seff — no GPU lines means no GPU How much VRAM did it use? seff's Peak GPU Memory Util How much RAM did it use? seff's Peak Mem Utilisation Why did it crash? Does it work at all? A job that waits, then svisit into it A batch job per attempt Why is it pending? squeue --me, the reason column

docs.title: Reading seff
docs.text:
Job Wall-time:          3%  00:00:31 of 00:20:00 time limit
Avg CPU Utilisation:   99%  00:00:30 of 00:00:31 core-walltime
Peak Mem Utilisation:   6%  243.67 MB of 4.00 GB
Peak GPU Utilisation:  16%
Peak GPU Memory Util:   2%  510.00 MB of 23 GB
Reading Means Do No GPU lines The job had no GPU Add --gpus-per-node GPU util under 10% The GPU did nothing Ask whether you need one GPU util 10–40% Starved More cores; check storage GPU util above 80% GPU-bound A faster card would help CPU 100% + GPU low Starved More cores CPU low + GPU high Too many cores Request fewer GPU memory under 25% Card too big Use a smaller one GPU memory over 95% Nearly out Smaller batch, or bigger card Wall-time 100% Killed, not finished More --time, or checkpoint

docs.title: The five mistakes
docs.text:
1. Forgetting --gpus-per-node. No error. The job runs on CPU, thirty times slower, and only seff will tell you.
  2. Confusing RAM and VRAM. --mem will never fix "CUDA out of memory".
  3. Trusting one nvidia-smi reading. It is a snapshot. Use nvtop or seff.
  4. Starving the GPU of CPU cores. The commonest inefficiency there is.
  5. Running fp64 work on an L4 or RTX PRO 6000. About twenty and five times slower than an A100, with no error message.

docs.title: The GPUs
docs.text:
GPU VRAM Per node fp64 Request Good for L4 24 GB 4 1:62 l4:1 fp32 work that fits. Shortest queue A100 40 GB 40 GB 3 1:2 a100:1 + --constraint=a100_40gb fp64 that fits in 40 GB A100 80 GB 80 GB 4 1:2 a100:1 + --constraint=a100_80gb fp64, large models, and NVLink across four GPUs H100 NVL 94 GB 2 1:2 h100:1 fp64 and the largest models RTX PRO 6000 96 GB 2 1:63 pro_6000:1 Large fp32/fp16 work. Not fp64

Take the smallest card your work fits in. Shorter queue, fairer share, same result.

docs.title: Before you queue anything long
docs.text:
#SBATCH --qos debug
#SBATCH --time 00:15:00

Run it short, seff it, then commit. Fifteen minutes saves days. Anything longer than a day should checkpoint (B3).

If you remember five things

  1. Software has to support GPUs. Requesting one changes nothing on its own.
  2. seff after every job. No GPU lines means no GPU.
  3. RAM and VRAM are different pools. --mem is not GPU memory.
  4. A GPU needs CPUs to feed it. Start at 2, then measure.
  5. fp64 work belongs on an A100 or H100. Nothing else comes close.

docs.title: 3. Is it really using the GPU?
3. Is it really using the GPU?
docs.text:
Lesson Objectives

  • Confirm Slurm gave your job a GPU
  • Confirm your software is using it, not just that it exists
  • Spot a job that has quietly fallen back to the CPU, and stop it happening

Questions

  • How do I know my job actually got a GPU?
  • How do I know my program is using it and not the CPU?

docs.title: Three things can be true
docs.text:
Asking for a GPU and using a GPU are separate, and they fail separately:

Slurm gave you a GPU? Your software found it? What you see Where the fix is No — CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES empty One line of your Slurm script Yes No Nothing. The job just runs slowly Your software install Yes Yes What you wanted —

The middle row is the dangerous one. Most GPU-aware software does not stop when it cannot find a GPU — it quietly carries on using the CPU. Your job runs, produces correct results, takes thirty times longer, and nothing in the output says why.

This chapter is two checks, in the order they answer those questions.

docs.title: Check 1: did Slurm give you a GPU?
docs.text:
When Slurm allocates a GPU it sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, listing the devices you may use. Every GPU library on the node reads it. You never set it yourself, but reading it is the fastest check there is:

echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"
Value Means 0 One GPU, numbered 0 0,1 Two empty No GPUs were requested, so you have none not set You are not inside a Slurm job

If this is empty, stop here — the problem is your Slurm script, and nothing downstream will fix it.

docs.title: Check 2: is your software using it?
docs.text:
This is the one that matters, and the one people skip.

Software How to ask PyTorch python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" TensorFlow python -c "import tensorflow as tf; print(tf.config.list_physical_devices('GPU'))" GROMACS gmx mdrun prints the GPUs it detected in the log header Most others The top of the program's own log. GPU-aware software almost always announces the device it picked

Is it even a GPU-capable build?

Software that cannot use a GPU is the most common reason a job that has one runs without it. For PyTorch, two values tell you:

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda)"
Output Means 2.13.0 13.2 A CUDA build. It can use a GPU 2.13.0+cpu None A CPU-only build. It never will, whatever Slurm gives it

A CPU-only build with a perfectly good GPU allocated is a software problem. No amount of fixing your Slurm script will help — B1: Getting your software running on a GPU is about fixing it.

docs.title: Running these checks together
docs.text:
The files for this chapter are in ~/gpu-training/first-job, and on GitHub.

The exercise folder has a script that makes all three checks and prints them side by side:

cd ~/gpu-training/first-job
cat check_gpu.py        # worth reading; it is short
sbatch check-gpu.sl

You can see check_gpu.py here. When you run check-gpu.sl, it will run check_gpu.py and produce the following output — here, from a job on Mahuika:

1. What Slurm gave this job
---------------------------
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES = 0
  This job may use 1 GPU(s).
  CPUs allocated: 2
  RAM allocated:  2048 MB

2. What the driver reports (nvidia-smi)
---------------------------------------
  NVIDIA L4, 23034 MiB

3. What your software reports (PyTorch)
---------------------------------------
  torch version:         2.13.0
  built against CUDA:    13.2
  torch.cuda.is_available(): True
  device count:          1
  device name:           NVIDIA L4
  compute capability:    8.9
  device memory (VRAM):  22.5 GB
  test calculation:      1000 (expected 1000)

  This job has a GPU and your software is using it.

The last line only appears after a real calculation has run on the device. Checking a flag is weaker than doing the thing.

docs.title: Not running on the CPU by accident
docs.text: Everything so far is a check you have to remember to run. The failure mode is that you forget, and find out weeks later.

docs.title: The signs
docs.text:
Sign Where you would see it CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES empty Your job's output torch.cuda.is_available() is False Your own check Your process missing from the GPU's process list nvtop (Measuring a GPU job) GPU at 0% while the CPU is pinned at 100% nvtop, seff seff shows no GPU lines at all Measuring a GPU job "falling back to CPU", "no CUDA device found" Your software's own log — grep for it The job simply takes far longer than you expected You, eventually

Grep your logs

Software that falls back usually says so somewhere, quietly, once, near the start:

grep -iE "cuda|gpu|fall.?back|device" my-job-1234.out | head -20

Worth doing once for any new package. You only need to find the line it prints on success to know what to look for on failure.

docs.title: Make the job fail instead
docs.text:
The reliable fix is not to check harder. It is to make a job that has no GPU stop, rather than spend two days quietly on the CPU:

at the top of your job script
[ -n "${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}" ] \
    || { echo "ERROR: no GPU allocated" >&2; exit 1; }

One line. A job that was going to waste a day of your allocation now fails in seconds and tells you why — whatever software it runs.

And record what you saw

Even when it works, leave the evidence in the output file — which GPU the job was given, and what it was:

echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES}"
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader

When you come back to a result in six months and wonder whether that run used the GPU, this is the difference between knowing and guessing.

Exercise: cause it, then catch it

  1. Run sbatch check-gpu.sl and confirm all three sections agree.
  2. Edit check-gpu.sl and comment out the GPU line with a second #: 
    ##SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1
  3. Submit it again and compare the two outputs.
  4. Now add the fail-fast guard above to the script, just before python3 check_gpu.py, and submit once more.
  5. Finally, the same mistake in a script that never checks: run sbatch forgot-the-gpu.sl, then seff it and your hello-gpu job from the last chapter.
What you should see at step 3 
1. What Slurm gave this job
---------------------------
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set but EMPTY.
  This job asked for no GPUs, so it has none. Add to your script:
      #SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1
  CPUs allocated: 2
  RAM allocated:  2048 MB

2. What the driver reports (nvidia-smi)
---------------------------------------
  nvidia-smi found no GPU for this job.
  No devices were found

3. What your software reports (PyTorch)
---------------------------------------
  torch version:         2.13.0
  built against CUDA:    13.2
  torch.cuda.is_available(): False

  PyTorch found no GPU because this job was not given one.
  This is a Slurm problem, not a software problem. Add:
      #SBATCH --gpus-per-node l4:1

Note what section 3 does not say. PyTorch is still a CUDA build — built against CUDA 13.2 — it simply has no device. Nothing is wrong with the software.

Had it said built against CUDA: None while section 1 showed a GPU, the diagnosis would be the opposite, and the fix would have nothing to do with Slurm.

What you should see at step 4 
ERROR: no GPU allocated

The job stops in seconds, and sacct records it as FAILED, instead of running to completion on the CPU. This is the version you want in your real job scripts.

What you should see at step 5

forgot-the-gpu.sl prints an empty GPU number, '', and nvidia-smi finds no devices. Then seff tells the two jobs apart: the hello-gpu job has two GPU lines at the bottom, and the forgot-the-gpu job has none. No GPU lines means no GPU. Measuring a GPU job covers seff properly.

It ends as FAILED, but only because nvidia-smi was its last command. Real software would have carried on, finished on the CPU and ended as COMPLETED.

Undo your edit before moving on.

Keypoints

  • CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES empty means Slurm gave you nothing. Fix the script.
  • Ask your software, not just the driver. A job can have a perfect GPU sitting idle beside it.
  • +cpu and version.cuda None mean a build that can never use a GPU.
  • Make the job fail when there is no GPU, rather than letting it run on the CPU for two days.
  • seff with no GPU lines means the job had no GPU.

docs.title: B2: Where the time goes
docs.text:
Beyond the basics

Not covered in the live workshop. It is the next step when seff shows GPU utilisation lower than you would like, and more CPUs did not fix it.

The scripts are in ~/gpu-training/where-the-time-goes/, and also on GitHub.

Lesson Objectives

  • Measure what fraction of your runtime a GPU could affect
  • Recognise when storage, not the GPU, is holding a job up
  • Know where on Mahuika to keep data, and how to read it quickly

Questions

  • My GPU utilisation is low, and more cores did not help. What now?
  • Where should my data live?

The introduction set out the ceiling: the work that is not on the GPU limits what any GPU can do for your job. This page is about measuring that split for your own job, and about the most common thing on the CPU side of it — reading data.

docs.title: Measure your own stages
docs.text:
cd ~/gpu-training/where-the-time-goes
sbatch phases.sl

The job runs a workload in four stages, twice, and reports where the time went. The first run, in phases-<JobID>.out, is reasonably balanced:

Where the time went
----------------------------------------------
  CPU  1. read input             3.0s   30.9%
  CPU  2. prepare                0.2s    2.0%
  GPU  3. compute                5.1s   51.6%
  CPU  4. write output           1.5s   15.5%
                             ----------------
       total                     9.8s  100.0%

The GPU was busy for 52% of this run.
A GPU 2x faster would cut 5.1s to 2.5s, saving 26% of the total runtime.

The second is the same computation, reading and writing much more (profile_phases.py --heavy-io):

Where the time went
----------------------------------------------
  CPU  1. read input             6.0s   42.0%
  CPU  2. prepare                0.2s    1.6%
  GPU  3. compute                5.1s   35.3%
  CPU  4. write output           3.0s   21.1%
                             ----------------
       total                    14.3s  100.0%

The GPU was busy for 35% of this run.
A GPU 2x faster would cut 5.1s to 2.5s, saving 18% of the total runtime.
Most of this job is not on the GPU. Speeding up the part that is cannot
help much - look at the CPU phases first.

Nearly two thirds of the runtime is now reading and writing, and no GPU on earth will do anything about it.

Run seff <JobID> afterwards, to compare the script's own figures with what seff measures from outside.

docs.title: Timing your own code
docs.text:
You do not need any special tools. Put timers around the stages:

import time

t0 = time.time()
data = load_and_prepare(path)
t1 = time.time()
result = model(data)            # the GPU part
t2 = time.time()
save(result, out)
t3 = time.time()

print(f"load    {t1-t0:6.1f}s")
print(f"compute {t2-t1:6.1f}s")
print(f"save    {t3-t2:6.1f}s")

Ten lines, once, and you will know more about your job than most people know about theirs. For non-Python software, the same thing:

/usr/bin/time -v ./preprocess.sh
/usr/bin/time -v ./simulate.sh

docs.title: What to do with the answer
docs.text:
If the GPU stage dominates (say over 70%)

The GPU is the bottleneck. This is the one case where a faster or larger GPU is the right answer — climb the ladder in Which GPU: will it fit?.

If preparation dominates

  • Parallelise it across more cores (How many CPUs).
  • Do the preparation once and cache the result, if it is the same every run. People re-decode the same dataset every epoch for months.
  • Consider moving that stage onto the GPU too, if it is arithmetic rather than parsing.

If reading and writing dominate

You are limited by storage. The rest of this page is about that.

docs.title: Where your data lives
docs.text:
Filesystem For Watch out for /home Configuration, source code, small environments 20 GB, and not for running jobs from /nesi/project Data and software you keep and use regularly, including large environments Your project's quota /nesi/nobackup Data your jobs read and write Not backed up; files untouched for 90 days are deleted

storage_quota shows how much of each you are using. The details are on Filesystems and quotas.

docs.title: Many small files are slow
docs.text:
A shared filesystem handles a few large files far better than many small ones. A dataset of a million small images — the usual shape of a machine learning dataset — is about the slowest thing you can ask of it, because every file costs a lookup before a single byte is read.

Pack them into fewer, larger files: a tar archive, or a format such as HDF5 that holds many records in one file. Most machine learning frameworks can read a dataset straight out of formats like these.

docs.title: Copy it to the node first
docs.text:
If a job reads the same data over and over — every epoch, say — copy it to the node at the start of the job and read it from there. On Mahuika, every job already has its own temporary directory, $TMPDIR:

  • By default, $TMPDIR is in RAM. It is fast, but everything you copy there counts against your --mem (How much CPU memory should I request?).
  • #SBATCH --gres=ssd gives the job a local 1.5 TB NVMe SSD instead, and points $TMPDIR at it. The GPU nodes have them. It does not count against your memory, but only one job on a node can have it at a time.
tar -xf /nesi/nobackup/<project>/dataset.tar -C "$TMPDIR"
python3 train.py --data "$TMPDIR/dataset"

Either way, the directory is deleted when the job ends, so copy anything you want to keep back out first. The Temporary directories page has the details.

Overlapping is often the biggest win available

The stages above take turns. They do not have to. If batch N+1 is read and prepared while batch N is computing, the waiting disappears:

taking turns:  [prep 1][gpu 1][prep 2][gpu 2][prep 3][gpu 3]
overlapped:    [prep 1][prep 2][prep 3]
                      [gpu 1][gpu 2][gpu 3]

This is what num_workers in a PyTorch DataLoader, or prefetch in a TensorFlow dataset, actually does — and it costs one argument. It is the background preparation from How many CPUs.

Exercise: your own workflow

On paper, break your own work into stages and answer, for each:

Stage What it does CPU or GPU? Roughly what fraction of runtime?

Then:

  1. What fraction of your runtime could a GPU possibly affect?
  2. If a GPU twice as fast were free tomorrow, how much would your job speed up?
  3. Is there a stage where a day of your time would save more than a better GPU would?

For most real workflows the honest answer to 3 is yes, and it is usually the loading stage.

Keypoints

  • Time your stages before you ask for better hardware. Ten lines.
  • If preparation dominates, add cores or cache the result. If storage dominates, fix the storage — a better GPU changes nothing.
  • Keep job data in /nesi/nobackup, and pack many small files into a few large ones.
  • $TMPDIR is in RAM unless you ask for --gres=ssd. Data you copy there counts against --mem.
  • Overlapping preparation with computation is often the cheapest large win available.
